articles.title: Suez Canal revenues double as vessel traffic rises in November
articles.summary: Suez Canal revenues have more than doubled in November 2026 compared with the same period last year, as the waterway records a recovery in vessel traffic amid the gradual return of major shipping lines. articles.body: Suez Canal revenues have more than doubled in November 2026 compared with the same period last year, as the waterway records a recovery in vessel traffic amid the gradual return of major shipping lines. According to figures released by the Suez Canal Authority (SCA) on 24 November, the waterway generated US$593 million in revenue since the beginning of the month, up 101.2% from US$295 million during the corresponding period in 2025. A total of 1,194 vessels transited the canal over the reporting period, compared with 886 a year earlier, representing an increase of 34.8%. Net tonnage also rose significantly, reaching 72 million tonnes against 37 million tonnes last year. The figures were presented by SCA Chairman Ossama Rabiee during a visit to the South Red Sea Shipyard in Safaga, where the authority marked progress on several marine construction projects. The improvement comes as international shipping companies gradually restore services through the Red Sea and Suez Canal. Recent developments include the return of additional Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd services under the Gemini Cooperation , alongside renewed transits by other major container carriers. The gradual return of container carriers is also reflected in Hapag-Lloyd’s recent activity. According to the Suez Canal Authority, 30 of the German carrier’s vessels transited the waterway between August and 23 November 2026, representing a combined net tonnage of 4.8 million tonnes. Although the latest figures point to stronger activity, the SCA has not provided a breakdown of container ship transits or revenue contributions by vessel type for the reporting period. SCA expands shipbuilding ambitions Alongside the traffic figures, Rabiee outlined plans to double the production capacity of SCA-affiliated shipyards and companies, targeting the launch of two marine units per month. The authority is also aiming to build 50 tugboats for export as part of its efforts to expand Egypt’s domestic shipbuilding industry. During the visit to Safaga, trials began for two AZM-class tugboats with a bollard pull of 90 tonnes each. These are the seventh and eighth vessels in an initial programme of ten tugboats. The shipyard also launched two REZK-class deep-sea fishing vessels, REZK 4 and REZK 5. Each measures 50 metres in length and is being built under the supervision of classification society RINA. According to the SCA, two additional AZM-class tugboats are expected to be delivered to Italy’s NERI Group, while a further contract covering four tugboats is under consideration. The authority views the expansion of domestic shipbuilding as an opportunity to strengthen Egypt’s marine engineering capabilities and increase exports of specialised vessels.

A total of 1,194 vessels transited the canal over the reporting period, compared with 886 a year earlier, representing an increase of 34.8%.
Net tonnage also rose significantly, reaching 72 million tonnes against 37 million tonnes last year.

articles.title: BIMCO puts ship-to-ship transfer costs on charterers
articles.summary: Shipping organisation BIMCO has released a new standard clause for tanker charterparties that places the costs and risks of ship-to-ship cargo transfers on charterers while preserving the master’s authority over vessel safety. Published this week, the clause covers conventional and gas tankers, including cargo...
articles.body: Operations Regulatory Tankers BIMCO puts ship-to-ship transfer costs on charterers Adis Ajdin November 26, 2026 0 0 1 minute read BIMCO BIMCO Shipping organisation BIMCO has released a new standard clause for tanker charterparties that places the costs and risks of ship-to-ship cargo transfers on charterers while preserving the master’s authority over vessel safety. Published this week, the clause covers conventional and gas tankers, including cargo transfers involving onshore and offshore installations. Under the wording, charterers ordering such operations will be responsible for the necessary equipment, regulatory permissions and associated expenses. Shipowners can also recover additional insurance premiums and other documented expenses arising from the operations, subject to prior approval from charterers. The clause allows owners to appoint a specialist mooring master or superintendent at the charterer’s expense when deemed necessary by the ship’s master. The master retains the authority to halt operations on safety grounds. The provision was originally developed for BIMCO’s CO2TIME 2026 charterparty, adopted in April for the emerging liquefied carbon dioxide shipping market. BIMCO subsequently opted to make the clause available separately for wider use across the tanker sector. The organisation stressed that the provision does not address sanctions compliance and should be used alongside appropriate sanctions clauses where necessary. articles.title: Polish offshore wind rules draw Danish shipowner backlash
articles.summary: Danish shipowners have raised concerns at EU level over new Polish vessel certification requirements, warning that additional inspections are making it harder for foreign operators to compete for offshore wind and marine construction contracts in the Baltic Sea. Industry association Danish Shipping has challenged...
articles.body: Europe Offshore Operations Regulatory Renewables Polish offshore wind rules draw Danish shipowner backlash Adis Ajdin November 26, 2026 0 76 2 minutes read RWE RWE Danish shipowners have raised concerns at EU level over new Polish vessel certification requirements, warning that additional inspections are making it harder for foreign operators to compete for offshore wind and marine construction contracts in the Baltic Sea. Industry association Danish Shipping has challenged rules requiring certain foreign-flagged vessels below 500 gt to undergo additional technical surveys before working in Polish waters, even where they already hold certificates from their flag administrations. The requirements primarily affect crew transfer vessels (CTVs), which carry personnel and equipment to offshore wind farms, alongside smaller construction and support vessels. Under Poland’s revised Maritime Safety Act, foreign vessels not covered by the SOLAS convention that operate in relevant Polish waters for more than 14 days in a calendar year must obtain a national operating permit. The application process includes technical verification by a recognised organisation, adding costs and potentially taking vessels out of service while inspections are carried out. Danish Shipping argued that the additional procedures duplicate existing flag-state oversight and create obstacles for companies seeking work on Poland’s expanding offshore wind projects. Høj Nordic Marine Contractor, based in Horsens, is among the operators affected. Chief executive Michael Normann said the rules were restricting the company’s access to the Polish market despite its existing operating experience in the country. “The rules make it harder for us to bid for projects in Poland,” Normann said. The company warned that the additional certification procedures could limit vessel availability, increase project costs and complicate contractual commitments. Danish Shipping’s executive director for sustainable ships and skills, Nina Porst, questioned the need for a second approval process and warned that similar national requirements elsewhere in Europe could further complicate cross-border operations. The association has raised the matter at EU level, arguing that countries should recognise existing flag-state certification rather than impose additional national approval procedures. Poland’s changes were introduced through amendments adopted in October 2025. Polish maritime legal specialists have linked the measures to concerns about insufficient technical oversight of some foreign-flagged vessels operating outside the main international convention framework. The Maritime Office in Gdynia has published an operating-permit procedure requiring evidence that foreign vessels meet safety requirements no less stringent than those applying to Polish-flagged ships. Danish Shipping previously challenged similar requirements in Germany, which were withdrawn in December 2024 following industry objections. articles.title: Trump administration’s case-by-case Jones Act review slows waiver shipments: analysis
articles.summary: The pace of Jones Act waiver shipments has fallen about threefold since the Trump administration shifted in August from a blanket waiver to case-by-case review of each request, a Platts analysis of US Maritime Administration data showed, as the administration extended the program Nov. 16 for another 90 days, through...
articles.body: Trump administration’s case-by-case Jones Act review slows waiver shipments: analysis in International Shipping News 26/11/2026 The pace of Jones Act waiver shipments has fallen about threefold since the Trump administration shifted in August from a blanket waiver to case-by-case review of each request, a Platts analysis of US Maritime Administration data showed, as the administration extended the program Nov. 16 for another 90 days, through Feb. 14. Cargoes moving under the original March 17 waiver and its May 18 extension loaded at an average of about 1.9 per day, peaking near 2.6 per day in June, according to the analysis. Under the Aug. 17 extension, which replaced the blanket suspension with individual review, shipments have averaged about 0.6 per day, as measured through the Nov. 23 report. The slowdown tracks what industry sources have described as a marked drop in waiver activity since the August change. The monthly pace did climb as the review process took hold — from a partial-month rate in August to about 0.7 a day in September and 1.0 a day in October — but remained below the average throughout the first two implementations of the waiver program. The first iteration of the waivers led to a dramatic redirection of US flows, with tanker-and-barge shipments of crude oil and petroleum products from the US Gulf Coast to the US West Coast reaching 4.43 million barrels in July, up from 1.26 million barrels in July 2025, an increase of roughly 252% year over year. The US saw a “remarkable uptick” in domestically sourced fuel shipments in the summer months, one industry trade group analyst said during an October policy briefing. That pace slowed in August due to “added regulatory uncertainty and burden.” “That doesn’t mean they have stopped flowing,” the analyst said. “It just means we have seen a remarkable reduction compared to the previous version of the process.” Political balance The American Maritime Partnership, which represents the US domestic maritime industry and has long criticized any Jones Act waivers as a threat to national security and US jobs, has characterized the case-by-case approach as “an improvement over the previous blanket Jones Act waiver,” while continuing to urge an end to the program. On Nov. 13, after the administration announced its latest extension, AMP issued a statement calling for a “prompt end” to the waiver and said the US should “continue scrutinizing all waiver requests under the case-by-case process to ensure that any approved waivers meet the statutory standard of military necessity and are not used to displace American vessels and American workers for routine commercial moves.” The Cato Institute, a Washington-based libertarian think tank, has tracked all 56 Jones Act-compliant US vessels and noted they have remained fully employed throughout the waiver period. “Foreign vessels have supplemented, not replaced, the Jones Act fleet,” Cato wrote. “With the Jones Act tanker fleet fully employed, each foreign-flagged voyage represents demand that would otherwise have gone unmet.” In all, MARAD has recorded 356 completed waiver movements since March 17 — 293 under the March/May waivers and 63 under the Aug. 17 extension. Gulf-origin trade still dominates The Gulf Coast remains the engine of the waivered trade, originating 271 of the 356 movements, or about 76%, reinforcing the region’s role as the primary seaborne supplier of US crude and refined products, the Platts analysis showed. The two largest lanes both run outbound from the Gulf, with 82 cargoes discharged on the Atlantic Coast and 78 on the West Coast. Cargo mix splits by destination. Gulf-to-West Coast movements skew toward light products, with 45 of 78 carrying gasoline or blendstock and seven more moving jet fuel, consistent with the West Coast’s shift toward a refined-product import model. Gulf-to-Atlantic flows run heavier on crude, with 32 of 82 cargoes carrying domestic grades bound for East Coast refineries. Shipments within a single region accounted for 101 movements, led by 56 within the Gulf — where crude, ammonia and fuel oil cluster — and 35 within the West Coast, concentrated in vacuum gas oil, renewable diesel and gasoline. Movement into the Gulf from other coasts remained limited, at 15. Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands drew 72 waivered voyages, 55 of them from the Gulf Coast — a destination that has grown as a share of the trade since the summer. The waivered voyages have together moved about 94.1 million barrels of crude and products, plus roughly 396,000 mt of cargoes quoted by weight, such as anhydrous ammonia and bitumen. The median parcel was near 300,000 barrels; the largest single cargo was 974,000 barrels of crude shipped from Louisiana to California via ship-to-ship lightering. Each movement cites a national defense interest justification, the standard statutory basis for suspending the Jones Act’s US-built, US-flag, US-owned and US-crewed requirements on domestic ocean shipping. The Trump administration first announced the waiver on March 17, as the US-Israel war on Iran led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz and has extended it three times since — May 18, Aug. 17 and Nov. 16. articles.title: Eight Organizations Sign Agreement to Advance GHG Emissions Visualization of Vessels
articles.summary: Nippon Yusen Kabushiki Kaisha, MUFG Bank, Ltd., Nagoya Electric Works Co., Ltd., ArkEdge Space Inc., Shimizu Corporation, City of Yokohama, Yokohama-Kawasaki International Port Corporation, and Yokohama Port Corporation signed a collaboration agreement on November 25 to develop remote sensing technology for measuring...
articles.body: Eight Organizations Sign Agreement to Advance GHG Emissions Visualization of Vessels in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 26/11/2026 Nippon Yusen Kabushiki Kaisha, MUFG Bank, Ltd., Nagoya Electric Works Co., Ltd., ArkEdge Space Inc., Shimizu Corporation, City of Yokohama, Yokohama-Kawasaki International Port Corporation, and Yokohama Port Corporation signed a collaboration agreement on November 25 to develop remote sensing technology for measuring greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from ships at a distance and bringing it into practical use. Under the agreement, the eight organizations will advance “True Emission Eye – Maritime,” a project to measure, visualize, and quantify GHG emissions from ships without physical contact. At Yokohama Port as the primary demonstration site, the project will conduct measurements on actual vessels and assess the accuracy of the technology. The project will also examine the specifications of the measurement and analysis system, potential applications, and opportunities for future business deployment. Nippon Yusen Kabushiki Kaisha (NYK Line), MUFG Bank, Ltd., Nagoya Electric Works Co., Ltd., ArkEdge Space Inc., Shimizu Corporation, City of Yokohama, Yokohama-Kawasaki International Port Corporation, Yokohama Port Corporation Background Technologies for objectively assessing GHG emissions from ships are becoming increasingly important as the international shipping industry continues its efforts to reduce emissions. GHG emissions from ships are primarily estimated based on fuel type and consumption. To complement these estimates, the organizations focus on remote sensing technology that enables direct measurement of GHG emissions from ships at a distance. The practical application of remote sensing technology has the potential to measure GHG emissions from outside vessels and improve the objectivity and accuracy of emissions assessments. Future wide-area observations using drones, satellites, and other platforms are also expected to help objectively visualize the decarbonization progress of individual vessels and contribute to a more transparent and fair market. Conceptual image of the system Overview of “True Emission Eye – Maritime” The project focuses on developing technology to visualize and quantify GHG emissions by leveraging the ability of gases, including carbon dioxide, to absorb and emit light at specific wavelengths. The approach combines ship exhaust data obtained using optical observation technology with relevant physical parameters, such as the distance to the vessel and weather conditions, to calculate emissions. The project has conducted tests at experimental facilities and measurements on Nippon Yusen Group vessels, both at berth and underway. At Yokohama Port, the project has captured infrared images of ship exhaust from locations including Osanbashi Pier and the Yokohama Bay Bridge Skywalk, and is comparing and analyzing these images with vessel data. Looking Ahead The project will continue conducting measurements on actual vessels, primarily at Yokohama Port, to improve the accuracy of its measurement and analysis technology through testing under various conditions and comparisons with vessel data. The project will also examine observation methods, including fixed-point monitoring at ports, and assess the technical requirements for observing GHG emissions from ships using satellites. The project will also explore the potential integration of satellite observations with ground-based data. Through continued collaboration, the eight organizations aim to bring the technology into practical use to help improve transparency in GHG emissions from ships and support decarbonization in the shipping and port sectors. Source: Nippon Yusen Kaisha 2026-11-26 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: IMO: Tackling fraudulent registries together
articles.summary: Strong national systems and international information sharing are crucial to tackling fraudulent registries and fraudulent ship registration practices, to protect seafarers, safeguard the marine environment and preserve confidence in international trade, IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez said on Wednesday, 25...
articles.body: IMO: Tackling fraudulent registries together in International Shipping News 26/11/2026 Strong national systems and international information sharing are crucial to tackling fraudulent registries and fraudulent ship registration practices, to protect seafarers, safeguard the marine environment and preserve confidence in international trade, IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez said on Wednesday, 25 November. Secretary-General Dominguez highlighted the issue following discussions in Kampala, Uganda, during the 9th Conference and Annual General Assembly of the Association of African Maritime Administrations (AAMA) (17-19 November), where heads of maritime administrations and ship registries from across Africa gathered under the theme, “From Policy to Practice: Advancing Africa’s Maritime Transport Excellence through Implementation, Cooperation and Innovation”. African countries target maritime fraud Bilateral meetings with transport ministers from several African countries provided an opportunity to hear from those who have experienced recent challenges with fraudulent activities. The IMO Legal Committee, at its 113th session in April this year, noted that 529 vessels had been identified as falsely flying the flag of a country, while almost 40 Member States had reported instances where their flags had been fraudulently used without their knowledge or consent. Several African countries are among those which have reported attempts by fraudulent operators to misuse their national identities, establish fake registries, or issue forged certificates ( see also the full list here ). Tackling “increasingly sophisticated” criminal networks Data submitted to IMO and a 2024 study by World Maritime University (WMU), the IMO International Maritime Law Institute (IMLI) and the UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) have documented the extent of the issue and emphasized the need for appropriate action. Criminal networks have become increasingly sophisticated. Fraudulent registry operators can create convincing websites, issue forged registration certificates, submit falsified documentation, and misrepresent themselves as legitimate representatives of maritime administrations. In some cases, countries that do not even operate international ship registries have discovered vessels claiming their nationality. Fraudulent ship registrations and fraudulent registries threaten maritime safety, environmental protection, security, the rule of law, and the welfare of seafarers. They provide opportunities for criminals to evade oversight, conceal ownership, bypass sanctions, avoid regulatory compliance, and engage in illegal activities under the cover of legitimacy. Vigilance needed IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez, said: “The vast majority of those who operate in the maritime sector do so responsibly. They deserve a system that rewards compliance, transparency, and accountability. Fraudulent registries undermine all three. We now have greater awareness of the problem, stronger international guidance and a growing commitment from Member States to act, including the IMO Guidelines on the registration of ships. What we need next is determined and coordinated implementation. There is no place for fraud in the global maritime community. Vigilance from all stakeholders is needed. Governments, shipowners, port authorities, classification societies, insurers, financial institutions, and seafarer organizations all have a part to play in identifying suspicious activities and protecting the integrity of the global maritime system.” IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez meets Uganda’s Cabinet Minister for Works and Transport, Hon Byamukama Fred, during mission in Uganda, taking part in the AAMA2026 Conference and Annual General Assembly in November 2026 To support information sharing, IMO’s Global Integrated Shipping Information System (GISIS) ship database is updated when information is made available that a ship is a “false flag”. Currently, 587 vessels are listed as “false flag”. The Guidelines on the registration of ships aim to assist new and existing flag State ship registries by providing practical measures to strengthen verification and due diligence, ensure accurate ownership records, and improve oversight of registration procedures. Source: IMO 2026-11-26 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: New pilot transfer requirements – prepare your fleet now
articles.summary: Our July Technical and Regulatory News highlighted the significant changes to pilot transfer arrangements introduced by the revised SOLAS Regulation V/23 and the new mandatory performance standards. Given the high level of customer interest and the many questions received, we are providing this follow-up news to...
articles.body: New pilot transfer requirements – prepare your fleet now in International Shipping News 26/11/2026 Our July Technical and Regulatory News highlighted the significant changes to pilot transfer arrangements introduced by the revised SOLAS Regulation V/23 and the new mandatory performance standards. Given the high level of customer interest and the many questions received, we are providing this follow-up news to complement our July 2026 update. Timeline The timeline for the new requirements: • 1 Jan. 2028: New pilot transfer arrangements installed from this date must comply with the new performance standards. All arrangements, regardless of installation date, must comply with the new requirements for operation, inspection, stowage, maintenance and familiarization. • First survey on or after 1 Jan. 2029: Existing arrangements on SOLAS ships must be verified for compliance with the new design, construction, securing and installation requirements. • First survey on or after 1 Jan. 2030: Corresponding verification is required for non-SOLAS ships. What does this mean for your fleet? Existing pilot transfer arrangements should be assessed well in advance of the applicable survey. Depending on the arrangements’ design, condition and level of compliance with the revised requirements, physical modifications may be necessary. Such modifications may include securing points, winch reels, stanchions, handholds and other parts of the pilot transfer arrangement. In some cases, compliance may require hot work or more extensive alterations, making early planning essential. Shipowners should therefore identify any necessary modifications in good time to incorporate them into the vessel’s next scheduled maintenance period or yard stay. For DNV-classed vessels, compliance with the retroactive requirements (RR) will be followed up through RR ref. 1088 for SOLAS vessels or RR ref. 1089 for non-SOLAS vessels. Why act now? Given the regulatory timeline and potential scope for physical modifications, DNV encourages shipowners and fleet managers to begin assessing their fleets now rather than waiting until the first survey. A timely fleet-wide assessment will identify compliance gaps, enable preparation of the necessary documentation, and integrate required modifications into planned maintenance and yard visits, reducing the risk of delays, unplanned costs or non-compliance. Recommendations DNV recommends shipowners and fleet managers to: • Identify affected vessels and arrangements across the fleet. • Assess existing arrangements against IMO Resolution MSC.576(110), supported by DNV’s Pilot Transfer Arrangement (PTA) Guidance for Managers, PIL 901. • Identify modifications early on, particularly work requiring structural changes, hot work or load testing. • Consider plan approval for complex or substantial modifications or where compliance is uncertain. • Coordinate modifications with planned yard stays where practicable. • Be prepared for the first applicable survey from 2029 onwards and ensure the vessel is ready for verification. Source: DNV, https://www.dnv.com/news/2026/new-pilot-transfer-requirements-prepare-your-fleet-now/ 2026-11-26 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.summary: Pacific International Lines (PIL) and Qingdao Port Group have marked a significant milestone in maritime decarbonisation with China’s first LBM bunkering operation for international shipping. PIL’s LNG dual-fuel container vessel, Kota Odyssey, received ISCC -certified LBM through a truck-to-ship operation at Qingdao...
articles.body: PIL and Qingdao Port complete China’s first Liquefied Bio-Methane bunkering operation in International Shipping News 26/11/2026 Pacific International Lines (PIL) and Qingdao Port Group have marked a significant milestone in maritime decarbonisation with China’s first LBM bunkering operation for international shipping. PIL’s LNG dual-fuel container vessel, Kota Odyssey, received ISCC -certified LBM through a truck-to-ship operation at Qingdao Port’s QQCTN terminal. This is the first LBM bunkering to an internationally-trading ship in China and marks Qingdao Port’s capability to offer green LNG molecules to international shipping lines. This is also PIL’s inaugural use of LBM fuel as the company works with partners across the maritime ecosystem to progress its goal of delivering more sustainable shipping solutions. LBM is a renewable fuel produced from organic feedstocks which significantly lowers carbon emissions when used in a ship’s engine. In this first phase, PIL is using it as a drop-in fuel for its LNG dual-fuel vessels without any modification to their machinery systems. Based on the well-to-wake (lifecycle) methodology, this batch of LBM is projected to cut carbon emissions by more than 70% versus conventional fuel oil. Compared to fossil LNG fuel, this fuel can also achieve GHG emissions reductions of around 70%. Abhishek Chawla, Chief Marine Officer, PIL said, “We are pleased to achieve this milestone in collaboration with our partners, Qingdao Port Group. This milestone demonstrates the flexibility PIL has built into our fleet renewal programme. With 28 newbuild LNG dual-fuel vessels ordered since 2022, we have the capability to progressively introduce lower-carbon fuels such as LBM into our fuel mix as these become more widely available. PIL’s objective is to provide our customers with a path to greener shipping solutions” Yijie Zhang, Head of the Energy Business Department, Ark Intelligence, Qingdao Port said, “This maiden biomethane bunkering service is a major milestone for China’s green shipping transition. It advances Qingdao Port’s development as a regional green bunkering hub. Our partnership with PIL reflects our shared commitment to maritime decarbonisation, and we will keep expanding renewable fuel options for international shipping.” Delivered to PIL in 2024, Kota Odyssey is an LNG dual-fuel container vessel deployed on PIL’s SWS service connecting Asia with West Africa. The vessel incorporates technologies to improve fuel efficiency and reduce emissions. The adoption of bio-LNG forms part of PIL’s broader decarbonisation approach combining fleet renewal, the adoption of energy efficiency technology and the progressive adoption of lower emission marine fuels. Source: Pacific International Lines (PIL) 2026-11-26 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: SeaVint adds “Ask the ship”, an offline AI that answers from the ship’s own SMS and manuals in International Shipping News 26/11/2026 SeaVint, a set of free desktop tools for ships’ officers, has released version 1.6 with “Ask the ship” — an AI assistant that runs entirely on the ship’s office PC and answers questions from the vessel’s own folders: the SMS, plans, procedures and makers’ manuals. How it works – The officer types a question in plain language (“How long is a hot work permit valid and who issues it?”). – The answer comes from the ship’s own files, with numbered references to the exact document and page, so it can be checked in one click. – Figures and dates in the answer are checked against the sources; anything not found there is flagged. – No internet is needed after installation and no ship data leaves the PC. There is no GPU requirement. – Installation is a one-time download of about 3 GB, or from a USB stick for ships with limited bandwidth. The assistant does not replace the officer’s judgement: it finds and quotes, the officer decides. The assistant is built on open-source components — llama.cpp (MIT licence) and Qwen3 language models (Apache 2.0) — with their licences shipped alongside the program. “On board, the answer is usually already in the folders — the problem is finding it during a busy port call,” said Alexey Krasikov, SeaVint founder and a serving Chief Officer on an LPG carrier. “Ask the ship finds the paragraph and shows where it came from, without sending anything ashore.” Availability SeaVint 1.6 for Windows is a free download at https://seavint.com/software . Existing installations receive it through the built-in updater. Source: SeaVint 2026-11-26 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

– The answer comes from the ship’s own files, with numbered references to the exact document and page, so it can be checked in one click.
– Figures and dates in the answer are checked against the sources; anything not found there is flagged.

Royal Wagenborg’s latest vessel design, EasyMax 2.0, places flexibility and efficiency at the centre of its future-proof concept. The Wärtsilä 25 engine’s modular architecture enables conversion to alternative low- and zero-carbon fuels as these become commercially available. Combined with its high efficiency and low fuel consumption, the engine provides a practical pathway for reducing emissions while protecting long-term asset value. “This new vessel type represents an important step in our ongoing fleet renewal and sustainability journey. The EasyMax 2.0 design builds on a proven vessel platform while incorporating new technologies that further improve efficiency and environmental performance. Wärtsilä’s engine technology is a key element of this concept, aiming for excellent fuel efficiency, operational reliability and the flexibility to support future sustainable fuel transitions,” says Niels Wage, CEO, Royal Wagenborg. Beyond supplying engines and propulsion solutions for numerous vessels across the fleet, Wärtsilä also supports Royal Wagenborg through a long-term service agreement covering its engines and propulsion systems. articles.title: Mediation in shipping disputes: an opportunity worth taking
articles.summary: Mediation is a confidential process in which an independent mediator helps the parties negotiate a settlement. Although participation may be ordered by a court, the decision whether to settle remains with the parties. Mediation can take place in person, with the mediator moving between separate rooms to explore...
articles.body: Mediation in shipping disputes: an opportunity worth taking in Marine Insurance P&I Club News 26/11/2026 Mediation is a confidential process in which an independent mediator helps the parties negotiate a settlement. Although participation may be ordered by a court, the decision whether to settle remains with the parties. Mediation can take place in person, with the mediator moving between separate rooms to explore common ground and, where appropriate, facilitating joint meetings. It can also take place online, where virtual rooms can be used. Courts are giving mediation greater weight Mediation in English court proceedings gained momentum in 1996, when the Central London County Court introduced its first mediation scheme. The Civil Procedure Rules 1998, which overhauled litigation procedures in England, actively encouraged mediation. The benefits to the public court system are clear: early settlement reduces court backlogs, administrative work and costs. It is therefore unsurprising that the courts have promoted mediation and used costs sanctions against parties that unreasonably refuse to engage. In recent years, the courts have taken a firmer approach. In Churchill v Merthyr Tydfil Borough Council [2023] EWCA Civ 1416, the Court of Appeal confirmed that courts can order parties to attempt alternative dispute resolution (ADR), including mediation. The Civil Procedure Rules were amended with effect from 1 October 2024 to reflect that ruling, with CPR 1.4 and 3.1 expressly addressing the court’s role in ordering ADR. In DKH Retail Ltd v City Football Group [2024] EWHC 3231 (Ch), the court ordered mediation despite the defendant’s objections that it was too late and had no realistic prospect of success. Interestingly, the parties subsequently reached an out-of-court settlement rather than proceeding to trial. What about arbitration? The position is different in arbitration. Many shipping arbitrations are conducted under the London Maritime Arbitrators Association (LMAA) Terms. Unlike the Civil Procedure Rules, the LMAA Terms do not give arbitrators an equivalent express power to order mediation. This reflects the consensual nature of arbitration and the parties’ control over the process. The LMAA questionnaire at the close of submissions, does however ask the parties whether they have considered if mediation might be worthwhile. In arbitration, as in litigation, an unreasonable failure to mediate may have adverse costs consequences. Against that background, several practical questions are worth considering when deciding whether to mediate. How likely is mediation to succeed? An estimated 21,000 cases went to mediation in 2025, and overall settlement rates remain high. According to CEDR, a leading mediation institution, approximately 87 per cent of commercial cases referred to mediation in 2025 settled, with around 70 per cent settling on the day and the remainder shortly afterwards. Online mediation, which grew out of necessity during the COVID-19 lockdowns, also remains popular. In 2025, approximately 38% of all mediations took place online; in the commercial litigation and arbitration sector, the figure was around 30%. Comparable statistics specifically for maritime disputes are harder to find. It seems likely that fewer shipping cases are mediated than in commercial litigation. Several factors may contribute to this. Many shipping disputes are subject to arbitration where there is less pressure to mediate than in court-based litigation. Disputes are a familiar feature of commercial life in some shipping sectors, making litigation or arbitration less daunting than in less litigious industries. In addition, where P&I or Defence Clubs fund legal costs, parties may also have less direct financial incentive to settle. Finally, the legal strategy adopted in a dispute may discourage settlement discussions. Together, these factors may mean that opportunities to resolve shipping disputes through mediation are being missed. How much will it cost? Mediation costs vary widely. The mediator’s fee is often a substantial component and is usually shared between the parties. For a two-party mediation, each party’s share of the fee for a one-day session is generally between £3,000 and £4,500. This usually covers a standard eight-hour day and often includes preparation. Additional time is normally charged at an hourly rate exceeding £400. As mediations often continue beyond the normal working day, the final fee may exceed the quoted daily rate. Legal representation can also account for a significant proportion of the cost. Solicitors generally prepare the written outline of the dispute and the bundle for the mediator. Parties can attend without legal representation, although this would be unusual in a shipping dispute. Where P&I or Defence Clubs represent each side, they could agree to attend without solicitors. Generally speaking, there is no need for a party’s barrister to attend. Mediation is not a court hearing and does not call for formal oral advocacy. Counsel’s attendance may be helpful in a high-value dispute involving complex legal issues, but even then, it would usually be sufficient for counsel to be available by telephone. In a highly technical dispute, an expert’s attendance may occasionally help clarify a particular issue, although this is rarely necessary. Venue costs can be reduced by holding the mediation free of charge at the offices of one party’s lawyers or P&I Club. However, a two-party mediation generally requires three rooms: two separate breakout rooms and a larger room for joint meetings with the mediator. The provision of that space may be a substantial commitment for a law firm. A specialist arbitration or mediation venue, such as the International Dispute Resolution Centre (IDRC) is likely to cost around £1,000 per party per day. Online mediation avoids the need for a physical venue. The total cost of mediation will often be in the region of £15,000 to £25,000 per party. That can be a worthwhile investment if the case settles but it is of course a substantial expense in a smaller dispute, for example one valued at less than $300,000. What are the benefits and disadvantages? The benefits are clear. Early settlement saves legal costs and management time. It also avoids the stress of continuing proceedings and can help preserve commercial relationships that litigation might otherwise damage. The disadvantages are less straightforward. The most obvious is the additional cost if the dispute does not settle. A subtler risk arises because productive mediation often requires both sides to recognise weaknesses in their positions. If one party engages constructively and the other does not, relations may deteriorate further. A party with no genuine intention of settling may also seek to use the process to gather information. The mediator’s role is to encourage meaningful engagement, but a mediator cannot create a willingness to settle where none exists. When is the best time to mediate? The best time to mediate is when both parties understand the facts and each other’s position, but before substantial costs have been incurred. Mediation often takes place after disclosure, although an earlier attempt may be worthwhile where the facts are largely undisputed. Earlier mediation offers greater potential cost savings, but it can still be valuable once the procedural steps are complete and the parties are awaiting a hearing. Hearing costs often represent the largest remaining expense and may justify a further effort to settle before they are incurred. What does mediation add to settlement discussions? Some disputes can be resolved through direct negotiation and a compromise on the figures. Where those discussions stall, an independent mediator can help each party examine the weaknesses in its own case and the benefits of settling it. For the party involved in the dispute, this may be the first opportunity to consider difficult points in detail with someone independent outside their legal team. Mediation also gives the commercial parties an opportunity to speak directly, without lawyers, if they wish. Their priorities may differ from the legal issues, allowing them to reach an agreement that resolves the dispute and potentially opens the way to further business. A negotiated settlement gives the parties control over the outcome taking away the element of risk that is always present if the case goes to a hearing. Summary Mediation is an important and often cost-effective means of resolving disputes, particularly when timed well and approached constructively by both sides. Our experience suggests that it may be underused in shipping disputes compared to general commercial litigation. This is unfortunate since it has great potential to save costs, reduce risk and preserve commercial relationships. articles.body: Clean Port Coalition Urges EU to Accelerate Port Electrification in Port News 26/11/2026 The Clean Port Coalition has written to the European Commission calling for ambitious EU rules to accelerate port electrification and shore power ahead of the AFIR review. Ahead of the upcoming Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR) review, the Clean Port Coalition (CPC), an alliance of industry, civil society, and maritime and energy stakeholders, has sent a joint letter to the European Commission calling for ambitious rules to scale up port electrification and shore power. While welcoming the EU’s recent Ports Strategy and Electrification Action Plan, the coalition warns that overcoming grid bottlenecks, financing gaps, and regulatory uncertainty requires decisive policy action. In the letter, the CPC outlines three core priorities for the Commission: • Provide a predictable regulatory horizon for the deployment of onshore power supply for all vessels calling at EU ports in the upcoming AFIR review, starting with the most operationally feasible segments. • Battery charging infrastructure: Introduce clear requirements to ensure sufficient charging capacity for Europe’s growing fleet of battery electric vessels. • Clean energy hubs: Streamline grid access and accelerate energy storage and flexibility measures to integrate ports into the wider electricity grid. Source: European Federation for Transport and Environment AISBL 2026-11-26 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Russian diesel exports rise despite Ukraine’s refinery attacks in Freight News 26/11/2026 Russian diesel and gasoil exports rose in the week ended Nov. 19, according to S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab) data, despite a wave of Ukrainian attacks on oil facilities that knocked out refining capacity and transport hubs. Russian refineries came under attack at least 16 times in the period between Oct. 30 and Nov. 23, with 14 different facilities suffering damage, according to reports. In addition, several Russian oil depots and oil transport hubs were targeted. Despite reduced refining capacity, Russia exported 552,000 metric tons of diesel and gasoil in the week ended Nov.19, up from 433,000 mt a week earlier. These were the highest weekly loadings of diesel/gasoil since early June, according to CAS data. Among Russian ports, 305,000 mt were loaded from Primorsk, up from 298,000 mt a week earlier. 100,000 mt were also exported from Novorossiysk, up from 33,000 mt. In addition, 60,000 mt was loaded in St. Petersburg, 45,000 mt in Ust-Luga, and 42,000 mt in Nakhodka, according to preliminary CAS data. Of these loadings, 119,000 mt of product were loaded for Turkey this week, down from 190,000 mt the previous week. 30,000 mt are expected to head to Brazil, down from 35,000 mt a week earlier, and 63,000 mt are preliminarily destined for Egypt, roughly unchanged from the previous week, with the remainder unknown. Overall, 462,000 mt of Russian diesel/gasoil has been loaded for Turkey so far in November, up from 284,000 mt in October, and the highest monthly loadings of product to Turkey since June, when 682,000 mt was loaded. During the same period in November, 132,000 mt of Russian diesel/gasoil have been loaded for Egypt, up from 64,000 mt in October. That was the highest monthly loading to Egypt since June, when around 240,000 mt was exported. Total loadings of Russian diesel/gasoil in November have reached around 1.5 million mt so far, higher than the October volumes of 1.1 million mt and the highest monthly loadings since June, when around 1.9 million mt was loaded, according to CAS. For comparison, Russian diesel/gasoil loadings were around 2.7 million mt in November 2025. Russia planned to export around 2.15 million mt of diesel in November, according to Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak. The statement came after a strike-free period of two weeks, before a major wave of attacks on refineries followed. Not a single vessel with Russian diesel was discharged in the US as of Nov. 24, despite a diesel deal announced by the US President Donald Trump at the beginning of October. “That diesel deal was a damp squib for a number of reasons. The big one is, of course, that the Trump administration issued an OFAC license which relaxed the executive order restrictions, but didn’t deal with the congressional sanctions,” Mark Hunting, a partner and sanctions specialist at international law firm Bracewell, said during a webinar Nov.24. The Malta-flagged medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes was heading to New York carrying Russian diesel and was due to arrive Nov. 7. But as of Nov. 24, it is still idling in the North Atlantic. “I think as these vessels are steamed toward the US, the people receiving them have been asking for legal advice. Some of them have been asking us for legal advice and they’ve been realizing quite quickly, actually, they can’t deal with this diesel,” Hunting said. “Of course, if President Trump really wants to get that diesel into the country, there are political solutions available to him. My best guess is that he wanted to be able to make the announcement on importing diesel for the purposes of market confidence on diesel prices coming down,” Hunting added. articles.body: Asia Offshore Renewables Hanwha Ocean pulls out of 800MW offshore wind project Bojan Lepic November 26, 2026 0 118 1 minute read Source Galileo Source Galileo South Korean shipbuilding heavyweight Hanwha Ocean has pulled out of an 800MW offshore wind development off the country’s southwestern coast. The company confirmed in a regulatory filing on Wednesday that it had decided not to participate in the first phase of the Jeonbuk Southwest Offshore Wind Expansion project after reviewing the conditions surrounding the development. Hanwha Ocean was part of a consortium led by Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP), which was selected as the project’s preferred bidder in June. According to local media, the estimated investment required for the project has increased from KRW4.8trn ($3.57bn) to around KRW6trn ($4.47bn) amid rising equipment and construction costs. Other members of the KHNP-led consortium include Korea East-West Power, KEPCO Engineering & Construction, KEPCO KPS, Doosan Enerbility, IBK Asset Management, KB Asset Management, Samil C&S, and Joong-Ang Heavy Industry. Hanwha Ocean’s decision follows several regulatory disclosures since July in which the shipbuilder said its participation in the development had yet to be finalised. articles.body: Dry Cargo Europe Greater China Taylor Maritime hit by shareholder revolt over pay Adis Ajdin November 26, 2026 0 134 1 minute read London-listed dry bulk owner Taylor Maritime has faced a shareholder backlash over directors’ remuneration, with more than 20% of votes cast against its annual pay report while the company winds down its shipping operations. The Ed Buttery-led outfit disclosed that 20.59% of votes at its November 25 annual general meeting opposed the directors’ remuneration report, although the resolution passed with 79.41% support. The vote saw more than 3.86m shares cast against the report, compared with approximately 14.9m in favour. Taylor Maritime’s board said it would engage with dissenting shareholders to establish the reasons for their opposition and publish an update within six months, in line with the UK Corporate Governance Code. The company’s separate directors’ remuneration policy received considerably stronger backing, with 98.33% of votes cast in favour. All resolutions at the AGM were approved. The opposition comes during the final stages of Taylor Maritime’s exit from shipowning, following a three-year disposal programme that has seen it sell almost its entire fleet. The company agreed in October to sell its last owned bulker for $15.1m, taking the number of vessel disposals since the beginning of 2023 to 56 and putting total proceeds on course to reach approximately $933m. The final owned-vessel transaction is expected to close in December. One ship remains on charter through a sale-and-leaseback arrangement with a purchase option, which expires in April 2027. Taylor Maritime formally adopted a managed realisation strategy in March, abandoning further fleet expansion in favour of selling its assets and returning capital to shareholders. The company has also been returning substantial cash to investors, including a fourth compulsory partial redemption of $45m in November. Buttery, meanwhile, has been building a private dry bulk position through his T3 Holding vehicle, which acquired interests in three handysize bulkers from Taylor Maritime earlier this year. The company’s next steps include further capital distributions and the proposed cancellation of its London listing once the winding-down process is completed. The developers are targeting commercial operations in 2032, with the infrastructure designed to transport up to 2m tonnes of hydrogen annually. The award marks NextGeo’s first contract with BarMar and expands its activities into the emerging European hydrogen infrastructure sector. articles.body: DSV and Cathay Cargo have signed a three-year agreement covering 4.5 million US gallons of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) produced in Asia, as the companies seek to support lower-emission air freight operations. The agreement covers 13,155 tonnes of SAF and is expected to support reductions of at least 45,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) emissions associated with air freight shipments. It marks the first long-term SAF partnership between the two companies, with Cathay Cargo becoming DSV’s first airline partner in Asia for expanding the use of sustainable aviation fuel across its regional network. By committing to fuel produced in Asia, the partners aim to strengthen demand for regional SAF production and support the development of a more reliable supply network. “This partnership creates long-term demand for SAF produced in Asia. It supports the regional production and supply needed to scale its use,” said Stefan Krikken, Senior Vice President, Global Air Product at DSV. Supporting sustainable aviation fuel in Asia The agreement builds on the companies’ existing commercial relationship and their cooperation through Cathay’s Corporate SAF Programme, where DSV has been a Diamond member. Under the programme, verified emissions reductions can be allocated to DSV regardless of where the fuel is physically used. Cathay Cargo will provide documentation covering the fuel’s journey from sourcing to aircraft refuelling, supporting the reporting and verification of the associated reductions. The partnership also aims to encourage further SAF production in Asia, where the availability of lower-emission aviation fuels remains limited. Longer-term purchasing commitments can provide suppliers with greater certainty over future demand, potentially supporting additional production capacity. “Scaling SAF requires collaboration across the aviation and logistics value chain, and this multi-year commitment reflects our shared vision to support its wider adoption,” said Dominic Perret, Director Cargo at Cathay. The latest agreement adds to DSV’s efforts to reduce emissions associated with international air freight. Earlier in November, the logistics group also announced a separate SAF collaboration with Google Cloud. The companies have not disclosed the financial terms of the new agreement or a detailed schedule for the fuel deliveries.

articles.title: UK offshore wind decommissioning estimates vary tenfold
articles.summary: Decommissioning provisions for UK offshore wind farms with similarly sized turbines can differ by as much as ten times, highlighting major uncertainties over the future cost of dismantling ageing installations, according to new research. A study by energy consultancy Xodus and its offshore renewables engineering arm...
articles.body: Europe Offshore Renewables UK offshore wind decommissioning estimates vary tenfold Bojan Lepic November 26, 2026 0 98 1 minute read Semco Maritime Semco Maritime Decommissioning provisions for UK offshore wind farms with similarly sized turbines can differ by as much as ten times, highlighting major uncertainties over the future cost of dismantling ageing installations, according to new research. A study by energy consultancy Xodus and its offshore renewables engineering arm Evolv Energies examined financial provisions disclosed by 37 operating UK offshore wind farms between 2019 and 2025, covering almost 2,500 turbines. The findings, published in a whitepaper titled Benchmarking Offshore Wind Decommissioning Provisions , revealed significant differences between projects. For turbines rated below 4 MW, reported provisions ranged from £180,000 ($236,000) to £1.83m ($2.4m) per turbine, while those above 8 MW ranged from £750,000 ($983,000) to £4.56m ($5.98m). Average provisions stood at approximately £900,000 ($1.18m) per turbine for smaller units and £1.5m ($1.97m) for the largest. The study also identified substantial changes over time, with one project’s estimated liability increasing more than sixfold during the review period, while others recorded only modest increases or downward revisions. Xodus said the variations suggest differences in engineering assumptions, removal requirements and accounting methods, making direct comparisons difficult. “Every offshore wind project is unique, and so we would expect decommissioning provisions to vary. What stands out, though, is the scale of this variation between projects using similar-sized turbines,” said Olivier Mette, head of advisory at Xodus. The findings come as Britain’s earliest offshore wind developments approach the end of their original design lives. Assuming a 25-year lifespan, 532 turbines included in the study will reach that milestone by 2036, rising to 1,285 by 2041. Operators will increasingly face decisions on whether to extend the life of existing installations, replace turbines or proceed with decommissioning. Xodus called for greater transparency in cost estimates and clearer regulatory guidance, particularly concerning requirements for restoring the seabed following removal. The consultancy stressed that reported provisions are discounted financial estimates, not definitive removal costs, and that existing offshore wind infrastructure could retain considerable value beyond its original design life. The tanker was carrying an estimated 7,000 tonnes of diesel, raising concerns about a possible spill in waters north of Ibiza. Initial inspections by the rescue vessel Guardamar Talía found no visible signs of pollution or floating wreckage. Spain has also deployed the specialist pollution-response ship Clara Campoamor , with aerial surveillance and satellite monitoring being arranged. MEPs have backed an objection to the European Commission’s proposed inclusion of Shree Ram Vessel Scrap and YSI Recyclers, both located in the Alang shipbreaking hub in Gujarat, by 377 votes to 214, with 24 abstentions. The vote came a day after eight international shipping associations, including BIMCO, European Shipowners, the International Chamber of Shipping, INTERCARGO and INTERTANKO, urged lawmakers to support the Indian yards. The industry maintains that existing European recycling capacity is insufficient to handle the anticipated increase in larger merchant vessels heading for demolition over the coming decade. Environmental campaigners welcomed the result, arguing that the beaching method used in Alang cannot provide adequate protection against pollution and hazardous waste. Ingvild Jenssen, executive director of NGO Shipbreaking Platform, said the Commission must apply the same environmental and safety standards regardless of where yards are located. As previously reported by Splash , the Parliament’s environment committee backed the objection earlier this month, despite both facilities receiving preliminary approval from the Commission following inspections. Their inclusion would mark the first admission of Indian shipbreaking facilities to the European list, opening up additional recycling options for EU-flagged tonnage. articles.body: A.P. Moller – Maersk and Morocco’s national railway operator, Office National des Chemins de Fer (ONCF), have signed a Memorandum of Understanding to explore the joint development of rail transport and integrated logistics solutions in Morocco. The partnership will assess ways to increase the use of rail for containerised cargo as the country’s import and export volumes continue to grow. The two companies aim to support more efficient and resilient supply chains while reducing reliance on road transport. Under the agreement, ONCF’s national rail infrastructure and multimodal expertise could be combined with Maersk’s ocean network and integrated logistics capabilities. The partners will examine potential solutions to improve connections between Morocco’s main ports and its industrial, commercial and consumption centres. “This Memorandum of Understanding is an important step to strengthen the role of rail within Morocco’s logistics ecosystem,” said Mohamed Rabie Khlie, Director General of ONCF. “By combining ONCF’s national rail infrastructure and multimodal expertise with Maersk’s integrated logistics capabilities and global ocean network, we can explore scalable solutions to reinforce the competitiveness and resilience of Moroccan supply chains,” he added. Sustainability will form another focus of the cooperation, with the partners examining lower-emission inland transport solutions based on rail. Expanding rail freight could also help relieve pressure on Morocco’s road network as cargo volumes increase. Morocco’s position between Europe, Africa and the Middle East, together with investment in infrastructure and the growth of its automotive and aerospace industries, has strengthened its role in international supply chains. The development of Tanger Med has also established the country as an important maritime and logistics hub. “Morocco has successfully established itself as a key trade and logistics hub connecting Europe, Africa and global markets,” said Guillaume Sauzedde, Managing Director Region Europe at A.P. Moller – Maersk. “Through our collaboration with ONCF, we will explore how rail can complement our ocean and logistics network and provide our customers with more reliable, efficient and lower-emission ways of moving cargo across Morocco,” he added.

articles.body: Hellmann Worldwide Logistics has partnered with robotics specialist Exotec to automate warehouse operations at Siemens Smart Infrastructure’s facility in Nuremberg, Germany. The project will introduce Exotec’s Skypod system, with around 35,000 storage locations planned for the initial installation and operations scheduled to begin in mid-2027. Hellmann has managed the Nuremberg warehouse since 2025, providing logistics services for Siemens Smart Infrastructure Buildings. The planned upgrade will replace much of the existing warehouse infrastructure with an automated system designed to handle increasing volumes while making better use of the available space. At the centre of the installation will be autonomous robots responsible for storing and retrieving goods and transporting containers to picking stations. The system follows a goods-to-person approach, bringing the required items directly to warehouse employees rather than requiring them to travel through storage areas to collect orders. Exotec’s Deepsky software will coordinate the robots and other equipment, using real-time data to prioritise orders and manage the movement of materials. The installation is also designed to expand alongside Siemens’ requirements, allowing additional storage locations and picking stations to be introduced as volumes grow. Automation to support future warehouse growth The project comes as Siemens prepares for further growth in warehouse activity at its Nuremberg site. By automating storage and order fulfilment, the company expects to improve efficiency, maintain service quality and accommodate higher volumes without relying solely on additional warehouse space. “By introducing this new automation solution at our Nuremberg site, we are creating the foundation to support future growth, continuously improve our operations and ensure a consistently flexible and high level of service for our customers over the long term,” said Daniel Schnuck, Director Global Warehouse at Siemens Smart Infrastructure. The installation also builds on the global warehouse automation agreement signed by Hellmann and Exotec in February 2026. That partnership established a framework for introducing scalable robotic systems across Hellmann’s contract logistics operations, with the Siemens project now providing a specific application of the technology. For Hellmann, the project extends its existing relationship with Siemens while strengthening its use of automation in contract logistics. Volker Sauerborn, Chief Operating Officer Contract Logistics at Hellmann, said the companies had worked together to develop a solution suited to the Nuremberg facility’s operational requirements. The financial value of the project and the number of robots to be deployed have not been disclosed.

articles.body: Freire Shipyard Celebrates Launch of New Greenpeace Vessel Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 25, 2026 © Greenpeace International Freire Shipyard celebrated the launch ceremony of NB 737 on November 25, 2026 in Vigo, marking a milestone in the construction of Greenpeace International's new flagship vessel. Designed to support environmental campaigns and scientific research worldwide while minimizing fossil fuel consumption, the vessel is scheduled for delivery by the end of 2027. With an overall length of 75 meters, the new sailing vessel has been designed to undertake demanding, long-range maritime operations, including campaigns in polar regions. Its design prioritizes energy efficiency, combining wind propulsion with an intelligent energy generation, storage and management system to minimize fossil fuel consumption. The vessel will feature a range of energy generation and storage technologies, including solar panels, battery storage systems, energy recovery systems and hydrogen fuel cells. These will be complemented by four dual-fuel internal combustion engine generator sets for electricity generation designed to use green methanol (MeOH) as their primary fuel, with small quantities of marine gas oil (MGO) used to initiate combustion. One of the key features of the design is the automated DynaRig sailing propulsion system, comprising two rotating masts with a combined sail area of 1,746 square meters. Under favorable weather conditions, this configuration will enable the vessel to circumnavigate the globe using wind power alone. In addition, while sailing, the propellers will be able to operate as generators, harnessing the vessel's movement to produce electricity. The aim is for the vessel to operate with minimal fossil fuel use from the outset, with a view to eliminating it entirely as the necessary supply chains and infrastructure become available. In addition, the vessel will feature onboard laboratories, systems for deploying remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) and autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), a helideck equipped to support helicopter operations, and four auxiliary boats that can be deployed even in challenging sea conditions. With the addition of NB 737, Greenpeace will expand its fleet, which currently comprises the Rainbow Warrior Ill, the Arctic Sunrise and the Witness, further strengthening its capacity to carry out environmental campaigns and scientific research in defense of the environment.

articles.summary: The US announced plans to impose a fresh round of tariffs on goods from China, the European Union and a dozen other economies under President Donald Trump’s push to restore sweeping global import taxes that the Supreme Court found unconstitutional.

BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI/Pool via REUTERS/File Photo By Alicia Diaz (Bloomberg) –The US announced plans to impose a fresh round of tariffs on goods from China, the European Union and a dozen other economies under President Donald Trump’s push to restore sweeping global import taxes that the Supreme Court found unconstitutional. The rate for imports from China would rise to 20%, in line with the country’s prior agreement with the Trump administration — though that rate could double to 40% if talks between the two countries fall apart, according to a senior US official. The official briefed reporters on condition of anonymity ahead of Wednesday’s announcement. Products from the EU will be taxed at 15% in compliance with the US’s deal with the bloc, though that could also rise to as much as 20%, according to the Office of the US Trade Representative. Tariffs will apply to items from economies the Trump administration accuses of overproduction in some domestic industries and hurting American companies. They are still subject to a public comment process and could change. A final action could come as early as January, the official said. The new levies mark the latest effort by the administration to reinstate an expansive tariff agenda that included country-by-country levies implemented using emergency powers. Those were struck down by high-court justices in February, forcing Trump to invoke other legal authorities to advance his agenda. It’s a politically risky move. Democrats swept to a landslide victory in the midterm elections earlier this month thanks in part to voter anger over the cost of living and disapproval of the president’s handling of the economy. China and the EU could also retaliate, though initial signals from them were muted. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a briefing earlier Wednesday that the prospect of new US tariffs on its exports was “political maneuvering” and said the two nations should work together to maintain their trade truce. The announcement appears to comply with the 2025 trade agreement between the US and EU, which capped tariffs at 15% on most of the bloc’s exports. As a result, the move likely won’t antagonize transatlantic relations for now. European Commission spokesman Olof Gill said “we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity” and added the bloc expects new levies to abide by the tariff agreement. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the new duties were designed to preserve existing deals while addressing overcapacity concerns. “A lot of these deals we made actually solve a lot of the problems we see in excess capacity or can go toward it,” Greer said Wednesday on CNBC. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we’re proposing. I think a lot of this is baked in.” Imports from Japan, South Korea, Switzerland — all prominent US trading partners — would be hit with a 15% rate. The number could go up to 25% for Korea and 20% for the other two, USTR said. Indian products would face a 17% charge if a trade pact with Washington is finalized, though that could increase to 25%. Several smaller nations in Asia were also hit. Similar expected measures aimed at Mexico and Norway were not included but remain under consideration, the official said. Greer said on CNBC the US has “had some very good conversations with Mexico” on the issue. The tariffs follow a probe that began in March into alleged excess manufacturing capacity, utilizing Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, a process seen as more resistant to legal challenges than Trump’s prior tariff wall. The tariff rates aren’t expected to surpass already agreed-upon levels in trade agreements with each economy. The move will test the tolerance of economic partners, who have largely held back from retaliating, opting instead to negotiate deals with the US to minimize their tariffs. That dynamic could be on display next month, when Trump meets again with his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, on the sidelines of the Group of 20 summit. Their trade truce is set to expire in January unless the two powers agree to extend it. “If we were to go beyond the 20% or something like that, they would view that as breaking our deal,” Greer said, The trade ambassador said Washington and Beijing are also “proposing to implement” tariff reductions under its new board of trade on around $30 billion of non-sensitive exports. Greer signaled that the new levy will not stack on top of existing duties of 10% or 12.5% under a separate investigation into negligent enforcement of forced-labor laws. “Those are not really additive,” he said on CNBC. For products eligible to be hit by both sets of duties, only the higher rate would apply, the official said earlier. The official added that there would be goods exempted from the tariffs, including oil and gas and food products that cannot be grown in the US. Other products that are already subject to sectoral duties, including tariffs on pharmaceuticals and critical minerals, are also exempted. After the Supreme Court loss, Trump immediately announced plans to rebuild his tariff wall under a different legal authority. Under the Section 301 framework, the president can implement tariffs following an investigation into allegedly unfair foreign trading practices. While Section 301 tariffs are seen as more legally sound and flexible than other powers Trump has eyed, they’re also more time-consuming. An earlier investigation under the same legal authority into policies around forced labor from US trading partners resulted in tariffs on some 60 economies. Those duties are currently facing legal challenges. The new tariffs apply to Bangladesh, Cambodia, China, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand, and Vietnam. USTR also announced it is raising tariffs on imports from Brazil, altering a previously-conducted trade investigation into the country’s digital policies and trade practices. The US is considering increasing the out-of-quota tariff rate on raw and refined sugar and proposing a 10% tariff on finished aircraft. The increased levy on imports from Brazil comes weeks after Trump ally Flavio Bolsonaro lost his presidential election bid to progressive incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy IMO The International Maritime Organization (IMO) is calling on shipping companies to make more training berths available to cadets, highlighting a longstanding disconnect between the industry’s need for qualified seafarers and the lack of opportunities for young people to gain the sea time required to enter the profession. In many developing countries, aspiring officers complete their shore-based maritime education only to spend years waiting for an onboard training placement, even as shipping companies struggle to recruit qualified personnel. In an announcement Tuesday, the IMO outlined efforts to expand its NextWave Seafarers initiative, which aims to address the bottleneck through cooperation between governments, shipowners and maritime training institutions. More than 80 participants representing over 25 countries gathered at IMO headquarters in London on November 20 to formally launch the second phase of the initiative and explore ways to increase the availability of onboard training opportunities. The program’s pilot phase, developed in partnership with Saudi Arabia’s Transport General Authority and national shipping company Bahri, saw 19 cadets from developing island nations and least developed countries complete their onboard training aboard Bahri vessels. The second phase aims to train at least 30 additional cadets, with women accounting for half of participants. The IMO also wants to recruit at least five shipping companies to provide training berths, laying the groundwork for a wider international partnership. The workshop examined practical barriers to cadet placements, including visa restrictions complicating crew changes, as well as the importance of providing a safe and supportive working environment for young seafarers entering the industry. The shortage of training berths exposes a fundamental challenge in addressing the industry’s workforce needs. Expanding maritime education alone will do little to increase the supply of qualified officers if graduates cannot secure the mandatory sea time needed to earn their professional credentials. Without sufficient participation from shipowners, the industry risks leaving a pool of prospective seafarers untapped at a time when it needs to attract and retain the next generation of maritime professionals. articles.title: Red Sea and Indian Ocean Nations Advance Plans for Combined Maritime Security Force
articles.summary: Countries bordering the Red Sea and Western Indian Ocean are moving toward establishing a combined maritime task force to combat piracy, strengthen regional security and protect commercial shipping across some...

Photo courtesy EUNAVFOR Countries bordering the Red Sea and Western Indian Ocean are moving toward establishing a combined maritime task force to combat piracy, strengthen regional security and protect commercial shipping across some of the world’s most strategically important waterways. The International Maritime Organization (IMO) announced that signatories to the Djibouti Code of Conduct and its Jeddah Amendment have adopted a new Regional Maritime Security Strategy and agreed to advance plans for a Combined Maritime Task Force (CMTF). The agreement was reached during a high-level meeting held November 11–13 in Antananarivo, Madagascar. The proposed task force would build on existing national and regional maritime security capabilities, improving coordination among participating countries. Governments agreed to develop the force’s legal framework and concept of operations in 2027. The initiative comes amid persistent threats to commercial shipping in the Red Sea and renewed concerns over piracy off the Horn of Africa, underscoring the need for greater regional cooperation in protecting international trade and seafarers. The broader security strategy covers the Western Indian Ocean, Gulf of Aden and Red Sea. Preparatory work began in Saudi Arabia in November 2024, with government representatives, navies, coast guards and maritime law enforcement agencies subsequently meeting in Mombasa, Kenya, earlier this month to finalize the framework. Originally adopted in 2009 in response to Somali piracy, the Djibouti Code of Conduct was expanded in 2017 through the Jeddah Amendment to address a wider range of maritime security threats. Somalia’s Minister of State Mohamed Abdulkadir Mohamed emphasized the human cost of attacks on commercial shipping during the meeting. “The protection of seafarers is not simply a maritime security obligation; it is a fundamental humanitarian responsibility,” he said. The meeting also marked a leadership milestone, with Tanzania’s Stella Katondo becoming the first woman elected to chair the regional initiative. South Africa will serve as deputy chair. While the agreement represents a significant step toward a more coordinated regional security presence, the proposed task force remains in development. The IMO has not announced a deployment timeline or details of participating naval assets. Finnish Border Guard/Handout via REUTERS ROME, Nov 25 (Reuters) – Italy has told Ukraine it was wrong to attack Russian ships in Libyan waters and warned Kyiv not to spread the war to new areas, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani told Corriere della Sera newspaper on Wednesday. “It was a mistake to violate Libya’s sovereignty,” Tajani said, adding that Rome had received no advance warning of the Ukrainian operations. “Italy was absolutely unaware of Kyiv’s intentions to strike in Libyan territorial waters, even inside a port,” said the minister, who is head of the coalition Forza Italia party. Ukraine has said the maritime drone attack against a Russian naval corvette and a cargo ship at the weekend was a legitimate act of self-defence. Tajani said he had telephoned his Ukrainian counterpart, Andrii Sybiha, to express his concerns, stressing Italy’s commitment to Libya’s territorial integrity. Another coalition party, the far-right League, also condemned the attack, calling it “unacceptable” and warning that it risked destabilising the north African country. Italy has been a staunch supporter of Ukraine since Russia’s 2022 invasion, providing military aid and backing European sanctions against Moscow. However, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government has sent mixed signals, with her own party firmly behind Kyiv while the League, led by Matteo Salvini, has repeatedly criticised continued military assistance to Ukraine. Tajani said that Rome would carry on supporting Kyiv’s sovereignty while seeking to prevent the conflict from spreading. “Italy will remain on Ukraine’s side. Ours is a strategic choice,” he said. articles.summary: A record 2,100-plus migrants arrived in Spain's Canary Islands over 24 hours in overcrowded boats, maritime rescue service data showed on Wednesday, prompting regional leader Fernando Clavijo to call for a European-level response to the crisis."The Canaries can't take it anymore.
